Tenders for the northern Ontario section of the all-Canadian natural gas pipe line are called by the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation and not by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.

Tenders were invited from 11 companies, being all the companies at present operating in Canada who were deemed capable of undertaking pipe-line construction of the type required for the northern Ontario section. The area is divided into five sections, referred to by letters of the alphabet and known as spreads. Five contracts have been awarded. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):,Minister of Agriculture,REPORTED IMPORTATION OF UNITED STATES CULLS,,,Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. The fruit, vegetables and honey
Inquiries of the Ministry regulations made under the authority of the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act makes the following provision with respect to apples being imported into Canada:
Apples shall not be below the requirements of Canada commercial or ""C"" grade.
The regulations further provide:

Importations from the United States of America may be considered in compliance with the foregoing if the accompanying United States government inspection certificate as endorsed by the United States inspector ""meets Canadian import requirements"" as follows: (a) apples shall meet the requirements of one or other of the following grades, namely, United States extra fancy, United States fancy, United States No. 1 or United States No. 1 cookers, of 21 inches minimum diameter or 234 box count size, and additionally the condition requirements of ""Standards for Export"" as defined by the United States Department of Agriculture-

Apples that meet the requirements for Canada commercial or ""C"" grade or comparable United States grade are not considered or classified as culls. Should it be found that after having entered Canada apples from the United States are below the certified or declared grade the importer or consignee is required to regrade the apples according to Canadian standards.

Recently two shipments of imported apples-and some apples given to me by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) came from one of these shipments-have been found to be below grade and have been placed under detention for regrading, but the inspection of imported apples from the United States indicates that the proportion of below grade apples is very small.

During the five crop years, July 1, 1952 to June 30, 1957, importations of United States apples into Canada averaged 744,000 bushels, while during the same period Canada exported to the United States an average of 1,493,000 bushels.

Paul Comlois (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):,Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys,SHIPPING,NORTH SYDNEY,DELAYS IN LOADING OF COAL,Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Ashbourne) asked me the following question:
Will the minister please look into the matter of delays occasioned to vessels loading coal at North Sydney for Newfoundland, and see if these loadings can be expedited?
The answer is as follows. Due to a wildcat strike and the 'flu epidemic there was a drastic cut in production during the past month in the North Sydney mines, causing
[Mr. Marler.l

delays in loading schooners for Newfoundland and larger carriers to St. Pierre and Miquelon. A check last night revealed there were schooners capable of carrying 3,500 tons of coal waiting in or near the port loading facilities at North Sydney.

A meeting was held this morning in Sydney attended by Mr. MacDonald, recently appointed executive vice-president of Dosco, Mr. Harold Gordon, vice president and general manager, Dominion Coal Company, Neil McLellan, chief of transportation, Dominion Coal, Captain J. L. Gullage, expeditor for Newfoundland government and schooner operators, the mayor of North Sydney and some members of the board of trade, North Sydney.

The situation was thoroughly studied and discussed, with the result that another meeting will be held this afternoon or tomorrow morning between Mr. McLellan, his operating staff and Captain Gullage and the committee of schooner operators to work out shipping schedules which are aimed at bringing shipping time back to normal by or before the end of this month.

,Progressive Conservative,,Paul Comtois,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=cccac50f-ae73-4d6d-9624-7f28a2a496ae&Language=E&Section=ALL

1913090,ca.proc.d.1957-11-18.45.1.7,1957-11-18,dcd2258a-b8c3-4099-bffb-7b24cce8341e,ca.m.9761,Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,WAR DEAD,GOVERNMENT CONTRIBUTION TO COST OF PILGRIMAGE OF MOTHERS,,From the supplementaries we have an indication of the additions to the original estimates that the minister wishes to have considered by the house, but he did give us some indication that there were in the other estimates items that he was not going to ask the house to give favourable consideration to, and there was the suggestion that perhaps he might have a list of those items prepared. It would certainly be a convenience, and it would probably make for a more expeditious consideration of the estimates, if we could have that information, if it were convenient for the Minister of Finance to have them tabulated so we could see what the general effect would be.
Perhaps when the minister closes the debate on the motion he might inform the house whether it would be possible for him to help us to that extent in the full consideration of the estimates.

I would like to make a brief statement about the attitude of the official opposition regarding this and the succeeding supply motions provided for by the rules. The house leader expressed the hope that it might not be necessary at this session to have six of
Motion for Committee of Supply those supply motions. We realize that this is not an ordinary session for which the rules were intended to have ordinary application.

In so far at least as the voting of supply is concerned, this is a continuation of the session that was interrupted by the general election. Except for the supplementary estimates, the other estimates are those which the preceding government recommended to the house at the last session of parliament and we would be quite prepared to facilitate their consideration. So far as the official opposition is concerned, we would be willing to forgo the right members have in ordinary session to six of these motions and we would even be prepared to agree to have all but one or two departments called when this motion is agreed to. The reserving of one or two departments would mean that there would have to be at least one other supply motion which would provide an opportunity to discuss whatever developments might have taken place in the meantime and would, I think, preserve the rights of parliament to retain such an opportunity for the voicing of grievances if they did arise.

With that reservation, we believe that the time of the house that can be devoted to motions to go into supply would be more profitably used in considering the estimates themselves than in a general discussion. That is all the more true in view of the fact that the time is now limited. The year for which these estimates have been prepared is well advanced and at a not too distant date we will be reaching the time when consideration will have to be given to the submission of estimates for the following year. I do not think it has ever been the experience of parliament to have two successive years' estimates under consideration at the same time.

For that reason and for the general reasons I gave when I spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the official opposition intends to offer no amendment to this motion to go into supply nor to support any amendment that may come from any other quarter. The reasons, I think, are obvious. There are only four more Mondays after this one before Christmas and though these motions do not, under the rules, have to be submitted on a Monday they are drawn in such a way that they envisage the use of the two first days of a week for the consideration of each one of these motions. If two days were taken to discuss each one that would take up so much time that the reason we gave for our stand on the address could not reasonably be expected to be implemented.
Motion for Committee of Supply

We felt it was the desire of the public that the government should have the opportunity to put before parliament the legislation it felt was required to implement such of its promises as, after its experience with the responsibilities of government, it feels can be implemented at this time. Although certain of these measures have been dealt with by the house, there are still others to come forward and we think it is in the public interest that there be a fair opportunity to have these measures brought before parliament to be dealt with and to be considered and disposed of.

Perhaps the leader of the house would also consider whether it would not make for the expeditious consideration of the estimates if an estimates committee was set up to which such departments as public works, northern affairs and transport could be referred inasmuch as there are many items of more particular interest to some members of the House of Commons than to others because of their local, immediate effect. That, it seems to me, would leave more of the time of the general committee available for the consideration of the portion of the estimates that are of more general application throughout the whole country.

I can assure the members of the government that, so far as consideration and disposition of the estimates are concerned, we are prepared to proceed in such a way as to leave the government a full and fair opportunity to have the house consider whatever legislation they feel it is their duty to submit in view of the campaign they waged. In order that such legislation may receive the consideration it deserves, we will be prepared to co-operate and to expedite the serious, businesslike consideration of the estimates so that the appropriation bills can be dealt with in the proper order and at the proper time.

Of course, we wish to reserve our right to criticize the present administration of government departments, but it will be our policy to expedite that discussion and to expedite the adoption of the items required to enable the government to carry on the business of the country without any impediment resulting from the fact that Christmas is coming upon us pretty rapidly, in fact at a rate as rapid as the shortening at the present time of the daylight hours.

We are also prepared to co-operate in

the proper and expeditious consideration of the estimates that have been placed before this session of parliament. But, Mr. Speaker, we are not prepared to abdicate our role as an opposition party in this House of Commons. We believe that even in a parliament made up as this one is, where no party has a majority, it is still desirable in the interests of democracy that there be a government and an opposition. If my hon. friends of the Liberal party are not prepared to be that opposition, we are.

We are prepared when there are opportunities presented by the rules of the house to state our grievances and, if necessary, to divide the house on some of these matters particularly where we feel the present government is falling down. We are amazed at the suggestion that because Christmas is coming or because new estimates may soon be prepared for presentation to parliament the time should be curtailed for the consideration of $5 billion of public money which is before the House of Commons in the form of the present estimates.

may be argued by both the Conservatives and the Liberals that these estimates are those prepared by the previous government. Quite true. But it is also a true statement, it is also a statement of constitutional and parliamentary fact, that those estimates were presented to this session of parliament by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). They are thus the present government's estimates. I know the minister made certain qualifications, but they are the present government's estimates. It is the present government that is administering the affairs of this country and is spending this money. We submit that members of parliament would not be doing their duty if they did not properly consider estimates involving this huge sum of money of the order of $5 billion.

We feel, Mr. Speaker, that these are important days in the history of democracy and that this is no time for an opposition in a democratic parliament to abdicate its function. I can assure you we have no intention of doing so. That is not to say we will delay unnecessarily the proceedings of the house. This does not mean we will not reach some compromise with the house leader in trying to arrange the business of the house. This does not mean that we are not prepared to surrender even perhaps some of our rights in view of the length of time that there is between now and next summer, shall I say, for two sessions of parliament. But let no

one imagine that we are going to surrender our rights in any wholesale fashion on these supply motions, nor are we prepared to agree, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) was prepared to do, to cut down to two or three the number of motions for going into supply.

We are not prepared to agree, as he suggested, to the calling of all the departments but two or three when this supply motion is concluded. Already too many grievances have piled up since this government came into power for it to be suggested that only one or two supply motions might be moved at this session of parliament. As I say, we are prepared to discuss these matters with the house leader in the usual way. It is no secret that we have already been doing that. But we are giving our pledge to the Canadian people that in so far as it lies within our power there will still be an opposition playing its role in this democratic parliament.

1913102,ca.proc.d.1957-11-18.46.1.7,1957-11-18,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre):,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,Before the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) rose on a point of order I thought I heard a suggestion from the front benches opposite that I was talking nonsense. We shall, of course, answer that charge by a number of references I shall be making to the record. Before I do so, perhaps in order to let the house know the terms of the amendment we propose to move, I might move it now. I may say that it spells out the grievance we have in mind and therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue):
That all the words after the word ""that"" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor:

this house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of taking immediately whatever steps are necessary so that federal payments under the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act will be available without delay to any provinces with hospital insurance plans in operation, as a further step toward the achievement of a nation-wide health insurance plan based on federal-provincial co-operation"".

In moving this amendment I want to make it clear that in our view the government has failed to take the steps that it should be taking to make sure that federal money will be available under the provisions of this act at the earliest possible date. Perhaps before I give the evidence as to the failure of the government to act on this important subject I should give hon. members a few interesting quotations from the record of the last session of parliament. This story of health insurance, and it is also true of hospital insurance, is of course a long one in the House of Commons and in the country generally. As a matter of fact, the Progressive Conservative party has had a fair amount to say about these matters for a number of years. I would say that for a few years they were a bit confused as to where they stood with respect
Health Insurance

and the senior Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Macdonnell). There you have 11 members of the present government, a majority of the present Conservative cabinet, who on April 10 of this year voted for an amendment to reduce that requirement of six provinces to something less, as a means of making it possible for this legislation to come into effect at the earliest possible moment.

At that time the premier of Ontario was saying that this was a ridiculous requirement, this requirement of six provinces. I might point out that he is still saying so, but in those days his view was being expressed here by those of us who were on this side of the house, by the Conservatives as well as by members of the C.C.F.
In summing up this part of my contention I would point out that there were three determined efforts made to get rid of this six-province requirement, one led by the

C.C.F., one by the Conservatives, and one which was a joint effort. We failed on those three occasions because of the adamant position taken by the Liberals, but nevertheless the record shows that the Conservatives were just as anxious as we were to get rid of that requirement as a means of making it possible for this legislation to come into effect at an early date.

Then the same hon. members opposite had a third point which they made during the course of that debate, which was that the coverage of the legislation should be broadened. In particular, and they agreed with us in this, they felt it should be made to cover those in tubercular and mental hospitals; and hon. members opposite, led by the present Prime Minister, who asked questions about the matter on the orders of the day, supported by others, came back to this theme, as we did, again and again. As a matter of fact, in the speech which the Prime Minister made on third reading he said he welcomed the legislation and congratulated Premier Frost on having brought the matter to a head, but that he still hoped that in the end, before the legislation was made final, it would be broadened so as to include coverage for mental and tubercular patients.

On clause 2 of the bill, as recorded at page 3239 of Hansard of April 8, the present Minister of Finance moved an amendment to change the terms of that clause so that instead of tubercular and mental patients being excluded from the provisions of the bill they would specifically be included. Likewise, on third reading of the bill, after our amendment regarding the six-province requirement had been defeated, the present Minister of Finance also on April 10, moved another amendment to refer the bill back to committee of the whole for the purpose of broadening the
clause which had to do with the extent of coverage, making it clear that the purpose of his amendment was to include mental and tubercular patients.

The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) was interested in the legislation, as well, and wanted the provisions to be broadened so as to include capital costs and depreciation as part of the shareable cost under the program. The present Minister of Agriculture made an interesting contribution to the debate with regard to the position of the Northwest Territories and, particularly, with regard to the position of Indians and Eskimos, making the point that it should be clear that they, too, were fully covered by the legislation.

In other words while there was the usual criticism which it is the right and duty of an opposition to make, though there were these amendments, and considerable discussion, the upshot of the whole debate as one remembers it, and as I have recognized again through reading it over the weekend, was that hon. gentlemen opposite wanted to see this legislation put into effect and its benefits made available to the people of Canada at the earliest possible moment.

Mr. Speaker, I now come to a fourth point which hon. gentlemen opposite made in the course of that debate. Perhaps they should remember some of the things they said, to which I will now make reference specifically, when they are a bit restive under some of the critical things now being said by such speakers as the hon. member for Essex East, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) and others who have sharp tongues. Hon. members opposite kept making the point -and I will prove this by chapter and verse -that it looked to them as if the former Liberal government was insincere, as if the former Liberal government did not really want this legislation to become effective. They reminded the former government again and again, as we did, that this question had had a history dating back to 1919, and that it had taken 38 years to reach this point. They pointed out also that the government had put into the legislation certain ""roadblocks"" which led a number of important people opposite to believe that this legislation was just something intended for the election, something which the former government did not really want brought into effect.

I turn for a quotation in support of what I am saying first to the senior Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I turn to the issue of Hansard of April 8. At page 3249 he said:
Why does the minister feel it necessary to have his hands tied absolutely in case his optimism is not justified?

He was referring of course to the present member for Essex East who had said, with his usual optimism, that he would get seven provinces or more, and was sure that the six-province requirement was not a roadblock.

hon. member is perfectly correct, they have done nothing. They have been in office since June 21. Plans have been made for a federal-provincial conference and hon. members are aware of the difficulty we have had getting statements as to whether or not the hospital insurance program will be discussed at that conference. We were told at first it would not be, and then we were told that it might be if ministers representing the provincial governments wished it to be discussed and when we asked whether the federal government would take the initiative in pushing this matter the reply was the same, ""There is nothing standing in the way; the provincial governments can discuss this matter if they wish to do so"". This is the kind of answer that is coming from hon. gentlemen opposite who said that my hon. friends in the Liberal party were insincere because they had put certain roadblocks in the legislation itself.

I point out there was no mention of the subject in the speech from the throne and there was very little mention of it in the official Progressive Conservative propaganda distributed during the election. In this respect we have something to say which is a little different from what we say with respect to many other items. In many instances we are asking the present government to implement the promises it made in the election campaign but so far as hospital insurance is concerned they were careful and cautious, relying on the impression they gave here last spring, the impression that they were the sincere ones, they were the ones who wanted something done. However, in the speech from the throne there was not a word about it nor has there been a voluntary statement on the matter by any minister of the crown since this house met on October 14. They have answered questions but it has
been extremely difficult to get any proper answers to our questions on this subject.

We have ascertained by the questions we have asked that no agreements have been signed by any of the provinces although six appear to have indicated their agreement to go along with this plan and it may be that the correspondence with Manitoba amounts to the agreement of a seventh province. Nothing has been done about the contention of the Conservatives last spring that coverage should be extended to mental and tubercular hospitals nor has there been any suggestion that the legislation be amended to cut down the requirement of six provinces so the legislation might come into effect with fewer provinces signing agreements.

Perhaps the most ominous thing that has happened in connection with this matter is what I would refer to as a false interpretation that has been placed upon certain words in the act by the new Minister of National Health and Welfare. I confess that the minisister did not take much part in the debate on this question in the last session; others of his colleagues were interested in health matters and he had other interests, but it does seem to me that he should have made himself fully aware of the background of the question I asked one day as to the difference between the words ""in force"" and ""in operation"". That background is extremely interesting and very significant. When the federal government made its proposals to the provinces in January last the paragraph having to do with a majority of the provinces representing a majority of the people agreeing to the plan ended up with these words:
-to take effect when the majority of provinces have such plans in operation.

The original proposal made by the former federal government was that what amounted to six provinces representing a majority of the people had to agree and those six provinces had to have their plans in operation before any money could be made available. Likewise, when the former minister of national health and welfare placed his resolution preceding the bill on the order paper on March 4, 1957, it read, as reported at page 1823 of Hansard of that date:

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize contributions to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund to provinces in respect of costs incurred by them in providing insured hospital and diagnostic services pursuant to provincial law and to agreements made in accordance with the said measure, to commence when at least six provinces, containing at least half the population of Canada, have entered into such agreements and qualified for the receipt of such contributions.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that was a confirmation of the original proposal that there had to be

what amounted to six provinces; that those six provinces had to agree to the proposal, and also that those six provinces had to have their plans in operation before any single province could get one dollar of federal money. Well, if the new Minister of National Health and Welfare does not know it, other Conservatives opposite do know that that was the cause of great concern to many people in this country who were interested in hospital insurance, and it was a cause of particular concern to their own Premier Frost of Ontario. Premier Frost said-I am paraphrasing his words, but I agreed with him 100 per cent and I still do-that it was silly and fantastic to say that no single province could get a single dollar until all six had their plans in actual operation. I think I am being fair to Premier Frost if I put it this way. He said on several occasions that that would mean that five provinces could go ahead and spend huge sums of money, put up the necessary buildings, get the bookkeeping machinery ready, get contributions started by the provinces, or by the people of those provinces, with a view to starting their plans on a certain day, but if the sixth province, say Prince Edward Island, did not have its plan functioning by that same date, then the other five provinces, even though they might represent the majority of the population of Canada, would not get a dollar of federal money.

Premier Frost characterized that proposal of the former minister of national health and welfare as silly, ridiculous and fantastic, and he was right. What happened, Mr. Speaker? We debated it in the house; we had questions about it time and time again, and I give full marks to the former minister of national health and welfare for meeting the objection, for changing the legislation. When the bill was finally brought down there was wording in it that was different from the wording in the resolution. It was different from the wording in the terms given to the provinces in January. There was wording that made it clear that the plan was to work in this way. As soon as six provinces had agreed to the program, and as soon as six provinces had their legislation on the statute books, in force, such as by being proclaimed, any one province which had its plan in operation would be able to draw its share of the federal money. As I say, that was made clear by the former minister of national health and welfare in the House of Commons on March 25, on page 2680 of Hansard. This is the way he put it:
When we get to the bill we will be able to discuss it much more effectively. The answer is that there is a difference. In the original proposal we said that when six provinces representing the
Health Insurance

majority of the people had plans in operation the federal government would pay, but the plans had to be in operation. It is now proposed that once we have the necessary authority we will conclude agreements with at least six provinces. If those six provinces sign and if they have the necessary legislative authority to implement their various schemes, as some now have, and if the law with respect to those schemes has been proclaimed or otherwise in force, that will be sufficient. In other words we do not have to wait for them to be actually in operation. When we come to the bill my hon. friend-
He was referring to me.
-will have an opportunity to discuss this.
Then I said this:

I thank the minister for that statement which is the most important one he has made all day. Is it clear that if six provinces have legislation in this field which has been proclaimed it will be possible at that moment for provinces having plans in operation to start drawing money from the federal government.

1913118,ca.proc.d.1957-11-18.46.1.23,1957-11-18,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre):,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,have already said that I give my hon. friend, the member for Essex East, full marks for having done something that governments do not like to do, for having made a change in the legislation from the time it was first drafted to meet a legitimate objection that had been pressed from the opposition side.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that that change was given statutory effect in section 6(2) of chapter 28 of the statutes of 1957, which reads as follows:

No contributions shall be paid under this act until at least six provinces, containing at least one-half the population of Canada, have entered into an agreement, and the provincial law in relation to those provinces is in force.

Now, Mr. Speaker, there is all the difference in the world between a law being in force and a health insurance plan being in actual operation, and the former minister made it crystal clear that that was the significance of the change that the former government made.

May I point out to my hon. friends opposite, many of whom are lawyers and must know how these bills are drawn, that the fact that there is a difference between the words ""in force"" and the words ""in operation"" is supported by this, that in the very next section, section 7, there is a provision that the money will continue to be paid so long as the provincial plan remains in operation. In other words, to start getting the money all that is necessary under the act is for six provinces to have the legislation authorizing their plans in force. Then, the money is paid to any province that has a plan in operation but, of course, you have to
Health Insurance

keep your plan in operation in order to continue to draw the money. But, Mr. Speaker, despite the fact that that was perhaps the major issue in months of consideration of this matter last spring, the Minister of National Health and Welfare rose in his place in this house on November 11, in answer to a question of mine, and said that his understanding is that ""in force"" and ""in operation"" mean the same thing. What a let down for Premier Frost, Mr. Speaker! What a let down for premiers of other provinces who counted on the terms of the legislation as it was passed last spring, counted on the statement made by the former minister of national health and welfare!

In our amendment, Mr. Speaker, we express the view that this government should take whatever steps are necessary so that federal payments under the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act will be available without delay to any province with hospital insurance plans in operation. What are the steps that the government should take? In the first place, since they already have the knowledge that six provinces have agreed, those six being British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, we contend that they should make definite and positive efforts to get agreements signed with these six provinces. So far as I have been able to ascertain there has not even been a master agreement drawn that these provinces might sign.

Other steps that we think the government should take include an effort to win some of the other provinces. At the last session the Minister of Finance said that the former minister of national health and welfare might have got more provinces in if his terms had not been so rigid. I remind this government that the government of the province of Nova Scotia, which is headed by a Conservative administration, has been pleading with this government for information as to where it stands on the question of hospital insurance. The other day I referred to two letters, which are on the table of this house, from the health minister of that province, one in September asking where the government stood, and another in October asking for an answer to the letter of a month earlier. There is interest on the part of a government headed by a Conservative administration which might be turned into agreement to the hospital insurance plan, if only a little interest were shown here at Ottawa.
I submit that in Manitoba there is a new interest in this matter. I know that the government we have in Manitoba has taken a new interest in a number of matters since

the 10th of June. The political climate has changed a bit. All right, let us take advantage of it. Here is a province which, until the 10th of June, was pretty cool to the hospital insurance legislation-now on the statute books-but which is now interested in it and yet despite its interest has difficulty in getting letters from the premier answered by the Prime Minister of Canada. There are at least two provinces other than the six which have already indicated their willingness to agree, that are showing an interest that might well amount to agreement. I think Mr. Speaker, it is pretty clear that it may not now be necessary to wipe out the six-province requirement because six, seven or eight provinces are ready to go along.

But what about this question of sincerity? My hon. friends across the way, speaking through the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), charged the Liberals with insincerity, with not wanting the legislation to come into effect. What have they done about it since then? What have they done to try to get those provinces that are interested to sign agreements? What have they done in terms of saying to Premier Frost, who has a tremendous program to launch that will cost a great deal of money, that if by chance there are not six they will introduce the necessary amendment to the legislation so that they can get started with fewer provinces? They took that position last spring and they took it very strongly. As I have already said, they took it three times, once on their own initiative, once when they supported us and once when it was a joint effort.

If they are sincere, if they felt they had the right last spring to challenge the sincerity of the Liberals, I suggest it is time for them to say to the house and to say to the country: We are out to get six, seven or eight provinces to agree if we can but if we cannot do that we are going to ask parliament to amend the legislation so this important program can go into effect with even fewer than six provinces. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the Prime Minister should immediately clear up the confusion that was created when that fictitious interpretation of the words ""in force"" was given on the 11th of November. That has been a cause of concern to Premier Campbell of Manitoba, a cause of concern to Premier Douglas of Saskatchewan and no doubt is a cause of concern to Premier Frost, although I do not have a direct quotation from him on the point since November 11.
But I would point out that Premier Frost did have something pretty strong to say about this matter, as reported in the Globe and Mail
of Wednesday, October 30, 1957. Under the heading, ""Frost Urges Repeal of Hospital Act Bar"", I note this:
The federal government-
The reference now is to the Conservative government.
-was urged last night by Premier Frost to repeal the section of the hospital insurance act requiring that six provinces introduce plans before there is a federal participation in costs.
Mr. Frost described the requirement as fantastic and silly.

I agree with him that it was fantastic and silly when the previous government put it in the legislation. It is even more fantastic and silly for the present government to rely on something which they opposed with all their might and main.

He said that although six provinces, including Ontario, have indicated they wish to participate in a hospital insurance scheme, restrictions placed in the act by the Liberals are tying the hands of the Diefenbaker administration.

Ottawa should throw out these restrictions and proceed on the basis of dealing with single provinces"", the premier suggested. ""If the act remains as it is we can go only so far. Ottawa should change the act so an effective date for starting provincial plans is established and leave it up to the provinces if they want to participate.""

As the federal act stands now only four provinces-British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, which already have hospital insurance plans in operation, and Ontario, have met its requirements. Unless two other provinces adopt the necessary legislation, Ottawa cannot share costs.
In all other instances where costs have been shared, such as old age security, the federal government has dealt with provinces individually, Mr. Frost added.
The departure from this established practice in the case of hospital insurance is a silly provision. It has no validity.""

I agree thoroughly with what Mr. Frost said as reported in the press of that date. I agree with the position he took last spring. My hon. friends opposite agreed with him last spring. What are they doing about it now? It looks to us, Mr. Speaker, as though this legislation is one of the inheritances which is an embarrassment to my hon. friends opposite. Oh, they liked to talk about health insurance when they could kick the Liberals around for taking 38 years to do anything about it, but now they are in power what are they doing? Oh, I suspect that they realize that they are going to have to do something about it in due course. I suspect they realize they are going to have this legislation in effect by January 1, 1959, because Premier Frost has set that as the target date so far as Ontario is concerned.

I give full credit, Mr. Speaker, to Premier Frost. He was concerned, not only that the legislation be amended so that Ontario could count on the money when it had its plan ready but he was concerned that provinces
Health Insurance

like British Columbia and Saskatchewan, which already had plans in operation, might start right away to draw their share of federal money towards their plans. It looks as though the federal government now in power has decided that British Columbia and Saskatchewan will not get any money towards their plans which are now in operation until the last possible date, and that date has been fixed for them by the Conservative premier in Ontario.

I much prefer the view Premier Frost has taken throughout the piece. Yes, he is pressing for action in Ontario but he has also pressed the rights of the other provinces. His point in this press report is quite correct, that just as the federal government has dealt with the provinces individually with respect to other social security matters, so they should deal individually with the provinces on this important issue.

I suggest also that we have a right to be apprehensive about this matter because of certain editorials that have been appearing in some of the newspapers of the country, mostly the Conservative press but in some Liberal newspapers as well. I have in mind, for example, the Winnipeg Tribune of my own city which has cautioned the government to be careful about the Martin hospital insurance plan. In addition to that kind of thing, we have this book which was sent to all members of parliament, I presume, entitled ""Underwriting Canadian Health, An Economic View of Welfare Programs"", prepared at the request of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. We all received copies of this book with a covering letter written by the general manager of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Montreal. It is a book that accepts the fact of welfare programs, including health and hospital insurance, but cautions the country against going too far.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, there are forces at work on the Conservative government of the day suggesting that they have to be careful about the welfare state, careful about welfare programs, careful about getting too deep into health or hospital insurance. With voices of that kind getting, as I have no doubt they are, the ear of the Conservative government, I think we have reason to be apprehensive whether or not early action is going to be taken to bring this important piece of legislation into operation.

Hon. members know where we have stood across the years. We have contended that there should be a nationwide program of health insurance with provision for provincial participation and administration. We have moved amendments to that effect in this
Health Insurance

house time and time again. Hon. members know that we want and feel that the Canadian people are entitled to much more than just hospital insurance. We feel that the day must come in this country when the care of the health of our people is on the same basis as education, available to all our people according to their need of that care rather than to the length of their purse. We shall continue to press forward towards the realization of a full health insurance program for the Canadian people.

We recognize that what we are pressing in this amendment is only for one step in that direction, but it is an important step. We contend that it is a betrayal of the Canadian people to have even as much delay as has taken place so far as this legislation is concerned. It was put on the statute books last April. Before the spring was out we knew six provinces had agreed. We had the story in the last session of parliament of the Conservative members fighting for this legislation to be put in a form so that it could be implemented early. We think we have the right, on behalf of the Canadian people, and we do it on this motion to go into supply, to demand early action on this important matter. My friends opposite condemned the Liberals for having made an election issue out of health insurance for seven or eight elections. They condemned them for having taken so long, from 1919 to 1957, to reach the point of presenting the Health Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to parliament. They condemned them for playing politics with health insurance, and particularly with this hospital insurance legislation. But it looks to us, Mr. Speaker, as though that is exactly what this government is now doing, toying with it, stalling and trying to find new interpretations of certain words in the act; leaving it to the provinces. They are doing nothing that is consistent with the aggressive battle that they waged here last spring.

The Conservatives condemned the Liberals for having made health insurance an election issue on a number of occasions, but it looks to us as though they are planning for this to be one of the issues in the next election whenever it comes. We are quite prepared to have health insurance or even the implementation of this hospital insurance legislation made an election issue. But we want something better than just the right to fight it out at an election, which we are prepared to do from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We want action on it, and we contend that the Canadian people are entitled to that action now. That is the purpose of this amendment, to ask this house to tell

the government to stall no longer but to take immediately whatever steps are necessary so that federal money will be available to provinces like British Columbia and Saskatchewan that have plans already in operation, and to the other provinces as rapidly as they bring their plans into effect.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as I have already indicated I place before the house the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue):
That all the words after the word ""that"" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following words be substituted therefor:

this house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of taking immediately whatever steps are necessary so that federal payments under the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act will be available without delay to any provinces with hospital insurance plans in operation, as a further step toward the achievement of a nation-wide health insurance plan based on federal-provincial cooperation.""

Hahn (New Westminster):,,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,With reference, Mr. Speaker, to your earlier ruling concerning the matter of procedure and the fact that we would be permitted to put forward our views on this question, may I do so now? I intend later, of course, to deal more specifically with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). With reference to the procedure, may I say that we in this group are not too happy to see the number of supply motions reduced, particularly since it was suggested also that the number of private members' days might likewise be reduced in order to complete the work of the house before Christmas. We are not particularly happy about the situation because we recognize that, to a degree, it means the termination of the supremacy of parliament.

Private members' days are the only opportunities afforded members to bring forward particular problems and grievances relating to their own ridings and to the nation as a whole. We are, therefore, rather reluctant to go along with the idea, although we do under the circumstances, fully realize that there is a difficulty at this time. This session of parliament, which is generally called the special session, has been called for the express purpose-I am not sure whether or not the express purpose is the immediate calling of an election-of introducing legislation that would appeal to the public. I would say, however, it is desirable legislation, and we have supported it.

However, we would look forward to the presentation of a budget before such a decision were made so that the people of Canada could decide for themselves whether or not we are in a position to expend $5 billion each year; whether we are going to be half a billion dollars in the red because of these particular expenditures or whether we can afford them. That is all I have to say with reference to procedure. We will go along with the idea provided we can see that the rights of the nation are protected and particularly that the rights of parliament are always protected in the future.
With reference to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I find it rather difficult to understand. As I interpret it, and my interpretation might be wrong, it reads thus:

-the government should consider the advisability of taking immediately whatever steps are necessary so that federal payments under the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act will be available without delay

I will not read the rest of it because it is that part which causes me some concern. As I interpret it, we are asking the government to accept the advisability of taking immediate steps to do certain things in respect of the act itself. I would suspect that the first thing the government would do would be to point out that the government is taking certain steps at this moment. The government has called a dominion-provincial conference and has invited certain representations from the various provinces. The government has indicated to those provinces that they are prepared to discuss the hospital insurance plan.

Under these circumstances it does seem to me that there is some redundancy in the amendment itself. If the government, of course, is not prepared to carry on and discuss hospitalization with the provinces then it is a completely different matter. One must, I know, really search to glean information
Health Insurance
on these things. It does take a considerable amount of reading and thought in an endeavour to discover exactly how the government feels with respect to discussing this problem.

Possibly the minister will be in a position to tell us more about it when he again takes his turn in this debate, as I trust he will, and will explain to us that the government is going to meet with the provinces to discuss this very problem, in which case this amendment of course would be meaningless because there could be absolutely no need for it as far as I can see. The government would have taken some action towards implementing this proposal.

This is a very important amendment, however, because it raises a problem which certainly has been discussed prior to the election, and is still being discussed today in my own province. I am sure the same is true in any other province having a hospital scheme in operation or, not having such a scheme in operation, having set up the machinery to put it into operation. It is important to the provinces to understand why the rules of the game have been changed.

For instance there is the interpretation placed upon the act, or a certain section of it, as was so well pointed out by the member who introduced the amendment. We should know why that particular rule has been changed. The implementation and bringing into force of this scheme is most important in my own province. We have in that province a hospital scheme which has been in operation for some years; we have certainly bene-fitted from the knowledge gained over those years and it does seem to me that if this scheme were made usable or operational at a very early date, before the six provinces set up their own schemes, then other provinces would gain from what we have learned in respect to the operation of the dominion-provincial scheme.

For this reason I very much favour the sentiment expressed in the amendment itself, as do all the members of this group. We are satisfied that this will probably bring to the attention of the government the need to do something more explicit, for instance by making it a point of discussion between the two levels of government in this country so that something definite can be done towards the implementation of the scheme itself across the nation.

Now with respect to the remarks made as to the sincerity of the government with respect to the setting up and putting into operation of this scheme, we can say all we like about the insincerity of the former government, but nevertheless the fact is that the act was brought into being by that
Health Insurance

government. The Conservative government of today, which complained so bitterly of the insincerity of the former government, is I would say just as guilty unless it changes its attitude in respect to implementation as quickly as possible. This point has been raised not only in the current session but also in the last session of parliament. I remember that so distinctly-as I am sure every hon. member who was in the 22nd parliament will remember without the necessity of referring to Hansard to prove the point. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) must also well recall that time and time again members from all parties doubted-possibly the Liberals did not doubt it too much-the sincerity of the government of that day with respect to this legislation. For that reason, the only way this government can prove that they are completely sincere with respect to this matter is to put it into operation in those provinces which have had the experience of running a hospital scheme. These provinces include Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.

From that experience the federal government and other provincial governments would gain sufficient knowledge so that the rough spots could be ironed out and those provinces which are thinking of setting up their own schemes would be in position to determine exactly what form of premium collection should be adopted and to deal with other small problems which might arise.

It is an acknowledged fact in my own province that we collect our premium in a different fashion from the province of Saskatchewan for example, which I understand has a yearly premium much the same as used in respect of ordinary insurance. We have a 2 per cent sales tax which goes towards paying for the hospital scheme. Now certainly it should be beneficial to a province which is deciding to enter this scheme to have an opportunity of choosing which of these schemes they prefer, rather than being forced to make an initial choice and probably losing a lot of money for the taxpayers because of inefficiency which might creep in as a result of inexperience.

In my own province for instance it is a recognized fact that we began with the collection of premiums, just as is the case of Saskatchewan today, but we found it undesirable to carry on in that way because it did not apply too well in our case. It was difficult to collect premiums; we did not have the same security for collection as did the province of Saskatchewan because more people moved about from job to job. We ran into many other difficulties when

for instance we found an individual who, having moved from one job to another thinking that his premium was paid, found that he did not have his insurance paid after all, and was therefore not eligible for hospital coverage.

Now it is true that these are small problems, comparatively speaking, but nevertheless they are an indication of the type of thing which must be met in each province and which that province's government must be prepared to act upon before setting up its own scheme. I would ask the minister to consider this question when he answers to the amendment and possibly confirm that this is a matter which is going to be placed before the dominion-provincial conference to be discussed at that time. In such a discussion it will make it possible for these provinces, by bringing out a few points, to come to a definite understanding as to when and how this scheme shall be put into operation.

My own thought on this subject, and I am satisfied that the members of this group concur in this viewpoint, is that the best way of dealing with the matter would be similar to the application for unemployment insurance when in the early stages we made it applicable on a certain basis to only one particular province. I think that was true of the logging industry in British Columbia. We had one province come in, and on the basis of the experience gained in its operation there we broadened it out as the years went on.

I do not think it is healthy for the people of this country to feel that either the present government or the former government is lacking in sincerity, or that their members of parliament are not sincere in bringing forward their suggestions. I am satisfied after listening to the representations which have been made in the past four years from the four parties in this house, including our independent members, that there is a particular desire to put a national hospital scheme into effect, and that such a scheme should be brought into being as quickly as possible so that all provinces may benefit from it.

Mr. Speaker, I have nothing further to add at this time, except that I hope the minister will take this whole question under advisement, and let us know in due course during the debate whether the government has changed its mind.

1913128,ca.proc.d.1957-11-18.46.1.33,1957-11-18,9fa12394-384b-4e7a-872b-8230b0e27dd7,ca.m.3489,Mr. Winch:,,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,Mr. Speaker, you will remember what I said but I do withdraw the term. This morning-now, do not prejudge me this time-I went down to our parliamentary library and asked the attendant if I could have the most authoritative English dictionary and the most authoritative United States dictionary. The attendant said the most authoritative English dictionary is Murray's New English dictionary and the most authoritative United States dictionary is Webster's International. I looked up the word ""treason"" in both volumes. Murray's New English Dictionary defines treason as ""betrayal of the trust undertaken by or reposed in any one; a breach of faith"". Webster's International dictionary describes treason as ""the betrayal of any trust or confidence"". Mr. Speaker, I bow to your request and I now say I charge the present government, according to Murray's New English dictionary, with a betrayal of the trust undertaken or reposed in it and a breach of faith, and according to Webster's International Dictionary I charge it with the betrayal of a trust and a confidence as far as hospital insurance is concerned. After hearing an outline

of the position taken by the Conservative opposition last spring as described by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, surely we can say there has been a breach of confidence and a betrayal of trust.

Hospital insurance which is now in effect in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan is something that is desired by all the people of Canada. Hospital insurance is a principle accepted by the previous Liberal administration and by the Conservatives when in opposition. To any fairminded, reasonable and honest person it was clear until the opening of this parliament the Conservatives believed in hospital insurance going into effect, let us say as soon as six provinces had agreed by legislation and by signature in Ottawa, and that payments would be made to any province having a plan in force or in operation, if you want to put it that way. However, no action has been taken by this government nor has any been intimated up to the present time.

I think we have no reason to apologize for asking why there has been no mention of the subject in the speech from the throne and no direct answers to any questions. This can be for three reasons only: (1) the government does not yet know what to do, as a government, as far as hospital insurance is concerned; (2) because of the partial fulfilment of promises made for increases in certain pensions the government is worried financially and wants to stall the additional cost that would be involved if hospital insurance were put into effect now; or (3) for the purpose of political expediency the government want to tie in with some other province in a provincial election and possibly in a federal election. None of the above reasons represents a sufficient explanation of the government's present attitude. Its attitude is unfair in view of the policy it enunciated when in opposition in that it is making the three provinces that already have plans in operation a sacrifice to political expediency.

As I said when I opened my remarks I have been interested in the question of hospital and health insurance for many years. In 1936 the province of British Columbia pioneered the field. A complete health insurance program was introduced in the provincial legislature by the Hon. G. M. Weir which was passed. Dr. Allon Peebles who now resides in Ottawa was made the first chairman of the health insurance commission. Although passed by the legislature the plan never went into effect because of sabotage by the medical profession in British Columbia. However this did not stop the province introducing a plan. Since that time it has

gone into the field of hospital insurance as have the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The taxpayers of those provinces have spent millions of dollars through these plans to give the people the benefit of overall hospital insurance.

At the last session of parliament the Liberal government, the official opposition and the other two parties in this house agreed that the federal government had a responsibility in terms of the health and hospitalization of the Canadian people. The act was passed and we all expected that it would go into effect speedily. Any dereliction of responsibility in putting the plan into effect as speedily as possible is penalizing not only the provinces which already have their plans in operation but is also deterring the other provinces which contemplate a hospitalization plan. I am convinced that a province like Ontario, with the hundreds of millions of dollars it will cost them to put their plan into operation, is contemplating doing so only if they can get a 50 per cent grant from the federal authority immediately. Unless there is a clear statement from the government that their policy is that a province shall receive federal payment as soon as the plan is actually in operation I am afraid that not only Ontario but the maritime provinces, which have agreed to come in, will be deterred in their planning. But if Ontario is to be given any assurance that when their plan goes into effect in January, 1959, they will be paid 50 per cent then, Mr. Speaker, it is only right, it is only just that Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia should be paid now because they have their plans in operation.

I know what it will mean in British Columbia. Most certainly we shall carry on, but what this government is doing-[DOT] unless they now establish the policy that the money will be paid in the immediate future-is that they are stealing around $18 million a year that rightfully belongs to British Columbia in order to fulfil some of their own election promises.

Hospital insurance is an important issue, Mr. Speaker. To the provinces that have not got it it is a blessing yet to come. The provinces that have it can reasonably and rightfully expect the declaration of principle of the Conservatives in opposition, now the government, that before this session ends, they will agree to contribute 50 per cent of the cost. We also expect, sir, that what was said by the Conservatives in opposition will be outlined by them as a government in the acceptance of half the cost of the mentally

ill and those who are suffering from tuberculosis.

1913139,ca.proc.d.1957-11-18.46.1.44,1957-11-18,5996b081-97f6-4bde-8dec-52df3dca3f76,ca.m.9560,Mr. Pickersgill:,,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,The legislation is there; it is on the statute books and it will come into operation, I assume,-of course, I have

It seems to me that that is a sensible provision. It seems to me that there is not any great likelihood that that outcome will not be realized during the course of 1958. To say the least this particular motion is somewhat premature.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made a great deal of the position he was taking that there must be a constitutional opposition in this house and he suggested that my friends and I had abdicated this responsibility and that he and his friends were taking this great burden from our shoulders. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the first duty of an opposition-the most essential of all duties, historically and in every other way, of an opposition in parliament-is to criticize the estimates. What the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon was that he thought it was more important that in the limited time available-the time is limited; we cannot change the calendar or at least I do not think we are going to try to do so-in this fiscal year we would be doing our duty better and more profitably by criticizing the estimates than by making academic speeches on academic motions which, if they passed, would defeat the very object they profess to be seeking to carry out.

There is not a word that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said on the motion today that could not have been said just as appropriately on the first item of the estimates of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) although it is true that he would have had to take two or three turns to say it under the rules. He could not have monopolized the time of the house for as long as he did when he was moving a motion of want of confidence. But perhaps in the interstices he could have obtained an answer or two from the hon. gentleman who is in charge of this department, which would have been a refreshing change.

It seems to me that the government can be justly criticized on two counts. It can be criticized for being dilatory about this matter. I think the most shocking example that has come to my notice-and perhaps it has come to my notice because I pay a little

bit more attention to the province in which I spent 30 pears of my life than I do to some others-was the history of the correspondence between the minister of health of Manitoba and the premier of Manitoba and ministers opposite. According to the facts that have been brought out with difficulty, in this house this session, in July the minister of health of Manitoba wrote to the then acting minister of national health and welfare, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks), and he received an acknowledgment but no reply to his letter. On August 1 the premier of Manitoba wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and he received no acknowledgment of his letter. In September, when the hon. member for Perth was appointed Minister of National Health and Welfare, the minister of health of Manitoba wrote to him and I am not sure-I am speaking from memory-whether he received an acknowledgment or not but he certainly received no answer to the questions he raised. On October 16 the premier of Manitoba wrote a second time to the Prime Minister asking for an answer to his first letter and to these other letters.

Several days later I asked the Prime Minister whether there had been any answers to those letters and he had no recollection of it. I admit that he gave a very polite and courteous reply as soon as he had a chance to check the matter. But I say that this is evidence-and it supports the evidence which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre himself produced-of a dilatory and rather irresponsible attitude, I do not say on the part of the Prime Minister who has multifarious duties, although I would have thought that a second letter from the premier of a province asking for a reply on as important a question as this would not have been brushed aside. However, it is surely a serious charge against the Minister of National Health and Welfare that four months after the government had come into office and well over a month after he himself had assumed office he had not yet had time to familiarize himself with important correspondence with his opposite numbers in provincial governments and with the premier of a province.

But what I think perhaps is an even more serious charge, Mr. Speaker, is the charge that the government has been extremely evasive in this matter. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is usually encyclopaedic in these matters, surprised me by failing to point out that, although the Prime Minister during the election campaign did not say much that is on the record about health insurance he did make two statements that are recorded in the press. Martin (Timmins):,,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,"Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this amendment I find it strange that so far we have had no speakers whatsoever from the government side of the house. As was so very capably pointed out by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), in times gone by, in fact as late as last spring, in this house and indeed right across this country from coast to coast during the election campaign various members of the present government had plenty to say on this matter. Therefore, as I say, I find it rather strange that at least to date they have been silent.

I had also looked forward to hearing the comments on this particular subject of my namesake in this house, the former minister of national health and welfare. I was quite surprised, not so much at the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who spoke or at least intimated that he spoke in behalf of the former minister, as at what he had to say when he did speak. I found it very difficult to follow just what he was trying to do, whether he was trying to support the government, whether he was supporting the amendment or whether he was trying to put forth the policy of the Liberal party on this matter, if any.

Even having noted the obvious determination of the Liberal party in this parliament to support the Conservative government, come what may, I may say I was really shocked to hear the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) refer to health insurance which so materially affects the health of this nation of ours, as it is being discussed at the moment, as something frivolous. I cannot see how any member of this house can maintain that the health protection of the people of this country is a frivolous matter which should not be raised and discussed in this house. Possibly, if as he intimated he was speaking for the former minister of national health and welfare, who in turn has been responsible for putting forward the policy of the former Liberal government in regard to health insurance for Canada, then that explains the reason why we have waited 40 years for the implementation of the Liberal promise of health insurance which was first made to this house in 1919.

I would like to say in conjunction with this amendment put forth by our party that there is a definite urgency to get on with this job of providing health insurance in this country. In addition to the reasons so well outlined by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I would draw the attention of this house to the fact that there are very powerful forces at work in Canada trying to stop or delay the health insurance as we now know it and to prevent it from spreading into a more comprehensive plan to cover the needs of the Canadian people.

To illustrate this point I would like to draw attention to this book which I believe was made available to all hon. members of this house. It is entitled ""Underwriting Canadian Health-An Economic View of Welfare Programs"", and it was done by a firm of consulting economists, William Loug-heed associates, Toronto, at the request of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and 96698-804
Health Insurance
the Canadian life insurance officers association. I would particularly like to point out an item contained in the preamble of the survey. This survey was for the express purpose of setting out:
-the urgent necessity of countering any tendency of the new hospital scheme towards ""natural"" growth into the areas or surgery, medicine, dental and nursing care.

Now there are scarcely two more powerful organizations in this country today than the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian life insurance officers association. In Canada they represent a tremendous amount of money, a tremendous amount of wealth and a tremendous amount of influence and I think in all fairness it can be said of both these organizations, judging from their past records, that it is business first, and nothing afterwards. I submit their primary interest is certainly not the health of this nation. As I say, their first consideration is that of their business interests.

We all know that costs in connection with health in this country are steadily rising, as they are in all other parts of the world. These costs are rising to the extent that people just cannot afford to be without health insurance and I submit that the motive behind these delaying tactics is to create a situation where everybody is going to be compelled to buy life insurance from these various insurance companies. I do not know just what costs were involved in conducting this survey but I assume that they were considerable. This survey had to be undertaken, the returns published and distributed over the wide field in which they have been distributed, and I think it is rather ironic that the money used to conduct the survey-to use its own words, ""for the express purpose of stopping a national health insurance plan""-was raised from the very people who pay premiums to these very insurance companies. In other words, the people's money is being used to cut their own throats.

I maintain that in addition to the reasons previously given, these points I have here outlined provide all the more reasons for getting on with this job without further delay. Paul Martin (Essex East):,,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether, before discussing this particular matter, I might take advantage of this the first day in the House of Commons of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) to extend to him a very sincere welcome. That, of course, again is a statement that I know he does not wish any of us to take seriously because it is in no way in accord with the observation made by the Leader of the Opposition. We shall exercise our right of constructive criticism.

What we are concerned about here at this time is to see that in the present unusual situation this government is given an opportunity of carrying out its election promises at the earliest possible moment. It is because

of that consideration that we have taken the stand which was stated by the Leader of the Opposition today and which has governed our conduct in respect of other matters involving amendments and other moves in this house that would have led to no other course than a dissolution of this parliament at this time.

On its face it looks like an innocent amendment and I have no doubt that it will be used by hon. gentlemen to my left in the far corner as an indication that only they and those who supported that amendment really are interested in seeing that hospital insurance in this country is furthered. I am sure that statement will be made by hon. gentlemen at what they regard as appropriate moments. But let my words now be associated with such declarations when I say that this amendment would be a very effective way of further postponing the day when we can have a real advance made in the matter of hospital insurance. What would be the consequence of it? The consequence of the acceptance of the amendment in this form would mean that this government would be defeated. That would mean that there would be no federal-provincial conference. That would mean that this government would not be in a position to carry on the kind of negotiations with the provinces that are necessary in furthering hospital insurance in Canada. That is what this amendment would mean. Instead of this amendment being a positive step forward for the implementation of hospital insurance, it would be a step that would at least suspend any of these negotiations which are necessary to the ultimate adoption of hospital insurance in Canada.
