1913183,ca.proc.d.1957-11-18.46.1.88,1957-11-18,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) points out the Prime Minister also said something along this line in Saskatoon while he was near home. I suppose that was a good place to say something that was obviously popular in Saskatchewan.

There are good reasons, therefore, in the face of this silence on the part of the government for those of us in the opposition to conclude that the government, if interested in hospital insurance, at any rate has not given great evidence of this interest or of its intentions. I feel that this particular debate today will serve the purpose of giving us an opportunity of urging the government to make a statement of its intentions, both as to Bill No. 320 as it now is on the statute books, and as it might be in the light of any changes which, in view of the position government members took from this side of the house, they might want to make.

The fact is that the correspondence between the Prime Minister and the various provincial premiers indicates that at the coming conference on November 25, understandably a fiscal conference, there is going to be little opportunity, if any at all, for a discussion of hospital insurance. Hon. members will recall that I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) on several occasions whether or not an opportunity would be afforded at that conference for provincial governments to discuss hospital insurance. The minister indicated that there should be no difficulty in having some kind of discussion with the provinces. But the correspondence between the provinces and the Prime Minister of Canada does not support that view. This correspondence clearly establishes that in the mind of the government this conference on November 25 is to be a conference dealing with fiscal matters and with fiscal matters alone. Of course, if a province wants to bring up the question of hospital insurance incidentally, in so far as it involves a very considerable expenditure on their part as well as on the part of the federal government, there could be no objection to that, I take it from reading the correspondence. However, the correspondence does not give any basis for discussion of further demands by the provinces on the federal government, for concessions or modifications in the existing law, except in a letter written to the premier of Manitoba on
October 29. Then, the Prime Minister did say there would be an opportunity at the dominion-provincial conference for discussing hospital insurance.

This letter preceded the letter that was sent to all the provinces later. We have to ask the Prime Minister which letter is to govern the situation in so far as this conference is concerned, the letter that was sent to Premier Frost and all the other premiers or the first letter sent only to the premier of Manitoba? The provinces are vitally interested in this. Manitoba is not one of the provinces that has, as yet, agreed to come in on the basis of the bill which was passed at the last session. Premier Campbell has said that because of the failure of the Prime Minister-undoubtedly a busy man-to answer his correspondence the acceptance of hospital insurance in Manitoba has been delayed. But for that delay there would have been progress made by that province in the matter of accepting the general offer laid down by the federal government in Bill No. 320.

Then we had a further complication that obscures the picture, or at any rate fails to give us a clear indication of what the government really intends to do about this matter on November 25. One of the members on this side, I think it was the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare if the t.b. and mental health patients were to be included in the coverage. The minister gave a reply that I think would lend itself to the interpretation that that might be done.

1913185,ca.proc.d.1957-11-18.46.1.90,1957-11-18,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,My hon. friend says, just like mine. If they were like mine, they were unequivocal. Then the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Deniset) asked the Prime Minister the same question on another day, and the Prime Minister said there was no commitment. On the one hand, we have a statement from the Prime Minister, and on the other that of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Now, the Minister of National Health and Welfare will not misunderstand me if I say that, much as I have respect for him and his authority as minister, I am bound to recognize that any declaration made by the Prime Minister must be regarded as having primacy in so far as declarations of policy of the government are concerned.

We have, therefore, these various contradictions which serve as a background for the building of a vacuum in so far as knowing what the intentions of this government really are. We do not know, for instance, whether or not they have abandoned the position that

they took when Bill No. 320 was under consideration, that the bill was acceptable, that the bill was a forward step but it was wanting in many particulars. The Minister of Finance, it will be recalled, moved an amendment to the effect that there should be included in the provisions of the bill certain features that were not included. We were told, not in an amendment, but in a whole series of speeches by hon. gentlemen when they were in opposition, that in addition to not covering tuberculosis and mental illness the bill was wanting because it did not provide for sharing alike with the provinces in the matter of depreciation. There were many speeches made by hon. gentlemen opposite that, in addition, the federal government should share in the cost of administering the scheme.

Now what is the attitude of the government with regard to these questions? Have they now decided, confronted with the responsibility which is theirs, that they do not propose to accept in government what they urged when they were in opposition? What is the reason that provinces like New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are not in the scheme? The situation before the election was this. Six provinces had accepted the federal proposal; they were the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island, Ontario and Newfoundland. The governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia were in intense negotiations, not only with the officers of the department but with myself. In answer to the question put by the member for Winnipeg North Centre, may I say that after the dissolution of this house and during the course of the election, I took advantage of my unsuccessful mission to certain parts of Nova Scotia to discuss with the premier of that province matters having to do with the acceptance by Nova Scotia of the hospital insurance proposal the federal government had made.

I can say that the negotiations I had with Premier Stanfield resulted in marked progress, and I had reason to believe that there was a likelihood of that province coming in. As a matter of fact the next day the premier of Nova Scotia made a statement in which he said there was no question that the Nova Scotia government would accept the proposal put forward by the federal government. Later I saw the minister of health for Nova Scotia and the minister of health for New Brunswick in Montreal, again during the course of the election, where I had a more successful mission, incidentally. They both indicated, in the presence of each other, the great likelihood of their provinces coming in. Now why have Nova Scotia and New Brunswick not come in since June 10; what reasons have they in their minds today for not having 96698-81J

accepted the proposal to which, at that time, it was evident they were giving favourable consideration?

Is it because this government has now taken some steps which are not acceptable to either one of these provinces? I do not know; we have had no statement on this matter from the government. We do know, however, that the government of the province of Nova Scotia has set up a second body to study from the point of view of Nova Scotia the advantages of this particular hospital insurance proposal of the federal government which is now part of the law of the land.

Has something developed in the meantime which causes them to feel they could not get from this government, under this law, the same kind of deal, for the extension of which the previous administration had received the approval of parliament? Do they feel that possibly because they share the same political conviction or ideology with the present government they might get a better deal? If that is the case then there should be no difficulty in the way of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) telling us just what is the situation.

However, here is the picture today, and it is a serious one, in so far as implementing this measure is concerned. Premier Frost has indicated that he proposes to bring in his act on January 1, 1959. It will be recalled that last winter the Prime Minister of Canada, in correspondence with the premier of Ontario, urged that premier to bring in his scheme at an early date and, while the then prime minister recognized that this was a matter exclusively within the control of the province of Ontario, he wanted Premier Frost to know that if he could bring in his measure before January 1, 1959, he would have the support of the federal government and, providing the necessary conditions embodied in the legislation were met, the federal government would be prepared to share with the government of that province the cost of hospital insurance in the province of Ontario.

Now Premier Frost has indicated the rates which will be charged to insured people in Ontario under his plan. That of course is a matter over which this parliament has no control or authority, but it does indicate that he is moving along with his scheme. Furthermore I know from my own conversations with Mr. Swanson, the head of the hospital insurance commission in Ontario, that the authorities were making and are making every preparation for the implementation of their measure-so far as they are concerned [DOT]-on the date Premier Frost has set for himself. But, under the act-and this is
Health Insurance

what the government must bear in mind-if when Premier Frost comes to set in motion his measure there are not the number of provinces with schemes in force, not in operation as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre properly pointed out no payments will be made by the federal government to the province of Ontario. No one would quarrel with the government of that province if there was a delay in the implementation of its scheme if they could not count on the federal government paying its share of this very laudatory but expensive proposition respecting the health of the people of Canada. So for that reason hon. gentlemen on this side of the house have every justification in pressing the government and prodding the government into action so that there will in fact be no delay on January 1, 1959, in the implementation of the scheme in the province of Ontario or in any one or other of the other five provinces.

Now the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says, as he said last year and on other occasions, that there is a way out of that situation. That way, he says, is for the federal government to pay money to any province which has a scheme in being. Now that looks like a very attractive proposition but I think, on analysis it is one that really cannot stand up. I say this because in British Columbia they have had a hospital insurance scheme for a number of years; they have had a hospital insurance scheme for a longer period of time in the province of Saskatchewan, and that argument would have applied equally four, five and ten years ago as well as, it is urged, it applies today or as it did when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made it last spring. The refusal of the federal government in that particular is based upon the sound proposition that it has no right to ask all the taxpayers of Canada to foot the bill for benefits-no matter how good they may be- for a minority section of the people of the country with respect of a particular provincial enactment. That is the principle behind our proposition and if it should eventuate that this present government changes its position in this particular, then I think other provinces will be in a strong position to say ""Well, what you have done""-let us say Ontario-""you should have done for us a long time ago.""

It is for those reasons that this government owes it to the house to tell us what negotiations have been carried on since they came into office, if any negotiations have in fact been carried on. We were told by the Minister of National Health and Welfare that his officers are ready at all times to discuss

these matters with the provinces. Well I say to him, of course the officers of the public services are ready at any time to discharge their duty, but that was not the question and it is not the question. What is this government doing to see that it makes itself available and what is it doing and what is the minister doing to further these negotiations with the provinces? That is the real question and unless we get a satisfactory answer to this interrogation we have the right to conclude that this matter of hospital insurance is going to be very considerably delayed indeed.

That is the proposition of which the province of Ontario should be aware, as I am sure it is, because last April in another room in this building I sat with my officials and those from the Department of Finance and from the province of Ontario, and it was pointed out by the provincial treasurer of Ontario at that time just exactly what the position would be in which Ontario would find itself unless we were energetic in our negotiations with the other provinces in getting them to accept the terms of Bill No. 320. The provincial treasurer said, ""We will have taken great steps in regard to other insurance schemes with labour, management, insurance companies and so on and there will be nothing but confusion in the province of Ontario unless we have some assurance at some stage""-which would have been about the month of September last-""that we can expect payments to be made by the federal government.""

Now that was the position at that time and we therefore sat down with the provinces to discuss with them the terms of the kind of master agreement that we would want to conclude between the provinces on the one hand and ourselves on the other. What progress has been made with regard to that kind of agreement?

When we left office we had exchanged the terms of the proposed clauses with various provinces. What has happened since that time? Has an agreement with Ontario been signed. We certainly would have signed an agreement, I am sure, by the end of June and certainly not later than the end of July.

I should like to say a word about the interpretation of the term ""in force"". The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked me a question on November 11 last. There were two or three questions. The final question on his part was as follows, as reported at page 942 of Hansard:

Mr. Speaker, may I ask a further supplementary question? In view of the fact that that is not the interpretation that was given to the last house by the former minister of national health and welfare, would the minister have appropriate inquiries made as to what is the legal meaning of those words?
My answer was:
Mr. Speaker, in my studies at the moment concerning the act I have every intention of doing that.
I have done that; I said I would study this. I have, and I have had a legal opinion. I should like to read section 6 subsection (2) of the act:

No contributions shall be paid under this act until at least six provinces, containing at least one-half the population of Canada, have entered into an agreement, and the provincial law in relation to those provinces is in force.
The legal opinion I have is as follows:

As a general guide I should think that the provisions of subsection (2) of section 6 as quoted above would be satisfied if the provincial statute has become law notwithstanding that the payment of benefits thereunder may by the terms of the statute be postponed to some future date.

Now, that simply means, I presume, that when it has become law in the province, no matter if they do not undertake to make a payment until some months in the future, it is still considered to be in force.

May I point out that some of the provinces have not reached the stage of development of their legislation where the question of being in force is at all pertinent. They just have not reached that stage. In an important matter such as this any final decision can be reached only after the actual legislation of the provinces concerned has been reviewed. Some may have to be amended; others, of course, have not got their legislation on the statute books yet.

There has been a lot of talk today about our being dilatory in pushing this legislation. Mr. Speaker, I can only say that we have been pushing this legislation with every intention of getting it into force as soon as possible. Let us remember that there are still many important points to be decided. Most of those important points must be resolved in consultation with the provinces. We have to work with them. We do not settle these things alone; they must be settled in consultation with the provinces.

All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that we are going forward with this legislation very rapidly. We have every intention of following it through without delay. We are going forward orderly but hastily. We do intend to come, and will come to a satisfactory and a beneficial conclusion which will react to the benefit of all Canadians.

1913245,ca.proc.d.1957-11-18.46.1.150,1957-11-18,ea775d4d-79fa-4519-baeb-7509d6fc7930,ca.m.2035,Mr. Zaplilny:,,HEALTH INSURANCE,FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES WITHOUT DELAY,,But there were two statements, one by the hon. member for Essex East and the other by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) to which I must take issue on a matter of principle. Both of them stated that in their opinion the chief reason why the government could not move until they had six provinces in agreement on this matter was-and I think I took the words down correctly- that in principle they object to all the people of Canada paying for something of which only a minority of the people could take advantage. When you lay that alongside the attitude of the same members of the previous government-and we remember the attitude they took with relation to the Trans-Canada pipe line, where they were quite prepared to have all the taxpayers of Canada contribute very handsomely to a few Texas millionaires who were going to have all the advantage,-then it is a little difficult to follow them in that principle.

The reason why I intervene in this debate at all, Mr. Speaker, is to try to get an answer to something which we have endeavoured to find out from the government, and which the minister in his reply has not yet disclosed.

The question is where the government stands in relation to its pledge made before and during the election campaign that, in their opinion, tuberculosis and mental illness should be included under this legislation.

We have a particular interest in this matter in the province of Manitoba because for some time it was given out to us in Manitoba by the provincial government that it was on this matter they were trying to make up their minds; in other words, that that was the reason for the delay by the province of Manitoba in declaring its intention as to participation under this legislation. Only very recently, according to a report in the Winnipeg Free Press, the minister of health and welfare in the province of Manitoba had something to say about this matter. I will quote from the report which reads in part as follows:

Hon. W. Bend, Manitoba health minister, said Wednesday Prime Minister Diefenbaker laid it down as ""a matter of principle"" for the Conservative party that national hospital insurance should cover TB and mental patients, and he added that the Prime Minister ""cannot break faith"".
Health Insurance

Those last three words are in quotation marks, ""cannot break faith"". It is not clear whether those last three words are a declaration of confidence or a veiled threat. But in any event in the opinion of the minister of health of Manitoba this present administration and the party that is in power is firmly committed to the inclusion of tuberculosis and mental illness under this legislation. On various occasions since this house met we have endeavoured to find out from the minister what the situation is and in the answers given, we have a contradiction which I should like to point out and I hope that some other member of the government,-perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself- will stand up before the debate ends and clear up this matter once and for all. I find that on October 31 as reported at page 599 of Hansard, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) asked the following question:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare whether it is the intention of the government to carry out the promise made in Winnipeg by the Prime Minister to include mental and tubercular patients in the federal hospital insurance plan.
Here was the answer given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith):
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member will find that it is the intention of the government to carry out all its campaign pledges.

He might have made that statement on the spur of the moment and he may have been trying to be facetious about it but I can assure him that that answer was very carefully noted in the press in western Canada and, as a matter of fact, as a result of that answer it was stated by the premier of our province and the minister of health in our province that they accepted that as a clear indication that it was the intention of this government to include tubercular patients and mental patients under this legislation.

But I find that on November 4 I addressed to the Prime Minister a question which arose out of actual reports in the Winnipeg newspapers saying that at last the government has announced in the house officially through its Minister of National Health and Welfare that it intended to include those two categories of illness under the act. I addressed the following question to the Prime Minister on November 4, as reported at page 701 of Hansard:

Has the government given a firm commitment to the province of Manitoba that tuberculosis and mental illness will be included in the federal government's share of the cost of the public hospitalization plan? If so, when was this commitment given and in what form?
The Prime Minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, there has been no commitment, direct or indirect.
[Mr. Zaplitny.l

At the time I wondered why he added those last three words ""direct or indirect"", because he could have argued there was no direct commitment in the sense that neither he nor any minister of his government had officially communicated with the government of Manitoba to inform them that the government had now adopted as a policy the inclusion of those two categories of illness. But when he said ""direct or indirect"", it could have had only one implication, namely that he was repudiating the answer that had been given by his own minister on October 31, wherein the minister had said it was the intention of this government to carry out all its election pledges; and in the context of that answer he was referring particularly to the question of the inclusion of those two categories.

It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that what the Minister of National Health and Welfare said on October 31 was contradicted or repudiated by the Prime Minister on November 4. That is the only impression that was left in my mind and that was the impression that was left in the province of Manitoba. That leaves the government and the people of Manitoba in exactly the same position they were in when they started. They still do not know what the position of this government is with regard to the inclusion of tubercular patients and mental patients. It is a matter of interest not only to the people of Manitoba but to all the provinces across this country. It is a matter which will have to be taken into account in the setting up of the legislation which the provinces will have to put on their statute books to deal with this matter, in the calculation of the cost, and in the calculation of what premiums if any they will have to pass on to the individual under this scheme.

I see no reason whatsoever why the Prime Minister, in the course of this debate, cannot rise in his place and clear up this one simple elementary question: Is it or is it not the intention of the government to do something during the course of this session to implement the promise which they so clearly made on many occasions to improve the present legislation by including tuberculosis and mental illness under the act? If the government will not disclose their stand on that question today, then the only inference we can draw from that fact is that they are backing away from the election pledges which they made and we even have reason to be suspicious, along with the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), that the government is backing away from the whole proposition of a national health insurance plan.

I certainly do not agree with the statement of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) that it is always necessary for a federal government to wait until the majority of the provinces comprising a majority of the people of this country are prepared to advance legislation before the federal government should be prepared to give a lead. It has been suggested to me by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that that was not the suggestion in the old age pension plan; that was not the suggestion in the amendments that were made in this very session to statutes

that required contributions by the provinces. Instead the government said that any time a provincial government was prepared to match such things as disability pensions, then the federal government was prepared to pay the money for the additional amount that could be provided. Even this government does not always wait until a majority of the provinces containing a majority of the people of this country are prepared to act.

I do not see that that is the role of the federal government, that legislation necessary to the welfare of the people of this country should wait until the provinces with a majority of the population are prepared to go ahead in a certain direction.
